fixed.q: In a max-heap:

fixed.q: Which is NOT a method to resolve collisions in hashing?

fixed.q: Keys 10, 22, 31, 4, 15 inserted into a table of size 11 with h(k) = k mod 11 and linear probing. Where does 15 go?
Searching an element in a sorted array using binary search takes:
fixed.w: Linear search O(n).

fixed.q: Which sorting algorithm has the best worst-case time complexity?
fixed.w: Quick sort worst case O(n²) (sorted input with first/last pivot), average O(n log n). Heap sort is also O(n log n) worst case.

fixed.q: The worst-case time complexity of quick sort is:
Which sort is most efficient on an already (nearly) sorted array?
fixed.w: Insertion sort best case O(n). Selection sort always O(n²) comparisons but fewest swaps (n − 1).

fixed.q: Which of these sorting algorithms is NOT stable?
fixed.w: Heap sort and selection sort are also unstable.

fixed.q: Which sorting algorithm is in-place with O(n log n) worst case?
fixed.w: Merge sort needs O(n) extra space.

fixed.q: The minimum number of comparisons needed to sort n elements by comparison is:
fixed.w: Counting/radix sort beat this because they don't compare.

fixed.q: How many passes does bubble sort need in the worst case for n elements?
fixed.w: Worst case O(n²) comparisons: n(n − 1)/2.

fixed.q: The worst-case number of comparisons in binary search of 1024 sorted elements is about:
fixed.w: ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 = 11. Some keys write log₂ n = 10; pick 11 if both appear, else whichever of 10/11 is offered.

fixed.q: Using the master theorem, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n solves to:
fixed.w: Merge sort recurrence. T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 → Θ(log n) (binary search). T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 → Θ(n).

fixed.q: T(n) = T(n − 1) + n solves to:
fixed.w: Sum 1 + 2 + … + n. T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 → Θ(2ⁿ) (Tower of Hanoi).

fixed.q: The Tower of Hanoi with n discs needs how many moves?
fixed.w: 3 discs → 7 moves.

fixed.q: Which algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that doesn't form a cycle?
fixed.w: Prim's grows the tree from a vertex. Kruskal uses union-find; O(E log E).

fixed.q: Dijkstra's algorithm fails when the graph has:

fixed.q: How many interchanges will happen when the sequence of letters of "SORTED" is sorted using bubble sort?
fixed.w: The number of bubble-sort swaps equals the number of inversions. For S O R T E D: S(4) + O(2) + R(2) + T(2) + E(1) = 11.

fixed.q: What is the maximum running time of binary search algorithm, when n = 12,000?
fixed.w: Binary search needs at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons: ⌊log₂ 12000⌋ = 13, so 14.

fixed.q: Consider an array of positive integers between 123456 and 876543. Which sorting algorithm can be used to sort these numbers in linear time?
o: Impossible to sort in linear time
fixed.w: All keys have a fixed 6 digits, so radix sort runs in O(d·n) = O(n).

fixed.q: A sorting algorithm is called stable if
o: It maintains relative order of occurrence of non-distinct elements
It takes O(n log n) time
It uses divide and conquer paradigm
fixed.w: A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original relative order.

fixed.q: Which of the following algorithm design techniques is used in the merge sort algorithm?
o: Divide and conquer, backtracking and greedy algorithm
fixed.w: Merge sort is divide and conquer.

fixed.q: Which of the following refers to the kind of problems that require the identification of the best solution to a search problem from a given set of solutions?
fixed.w: Problems that need the best solution from a set of feasible solutions are optimisation problems.

fixed.q: Which of the following is NOT an application of Divide and Conquer?
fixed.w: All-pairs shortest path (Floyd–Warshall) uses dynamic programming; the others are divide and conquer.

fixed.q: What are the solutions for the following sum-of-subsets problem? w[1:5] = {2, 7, 8, 9, 15}; required sum = 17. (1 means the item is included, 0 means it is excluded.)
In the dynamic programming approach, the value of an optimal solution is computed in:
fixed.w: Classic DP (tabulation) builds solutions from the smallest subproblems up. The top-down version is called memoisation.

fixed.q: What is the product of the following matrices using Strassen's matrix multiplication algorithm? A = [1 3; 5 7], B = [8 4; 6 2]
fixed.w: Strassen gives the same product as ordinary multiplication: C11 = 8 + 18 = 26, C12 = 4 + 6 = 10, C21 = 40 + 42 = 82, C22 = 20 + 14 = 34.

fixed.q: Which of the following is a correct time complexity to solve the 0/1 knapsack problem, where n and w represent the number of items and the capacity of the knapsack respectively?
fixed.w: The DP table has n × w cells, each filled in O(1), so it is O(nw) (pseudo-polynomial).

fixed.q: Assembly line scheduling and Longest Common Subsequence problems are examples of ____.
o: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming respectively
Dynamic Programming and Branch and Bound respectively

fixed.q: Which characteristic of an algorithm refers to 'each instruction is clear and unambiguous'?
fixed.w: Definiteness means every step is precise and unambiguous.

fixed.q: Which of the following is the correct recurrence for the worst case of QuickSort?
fixed.w: In the worst case the pivot is the smallest or largest element, leaving subproblems of size n−1 and 0, which gives O(n²).

fixed.q:
What is the time complexity of the following recursive function?
int ComputFun(int n) { if (n <= 2) return 1; else return (ComputFun(floor(sqrt(n))) + n); }
fixed.w: T(n) = T(√n) + n. The work n + √n + n^(1/4) + … is dominated by the first term, so it is Θ(n). The recursion depth is only log log n, but each call adds n at the top level.
Worst case (n prime) the loop runs about √n times. Best case (n even) it exits after 1 iteration (GATE 2007).

fixed.q: An algorithm is made up of two modules M1 and M2. If the order of M1 is f(n) and of M2 is g(n), then the order of the algorithm is
fixed.w: Running modules one after the other costs O(f + g) = O(max(f, g)).

fixed.q: The running time of an algorithm T(n), where n is the input size, is given by T(n) = 8T(n/2) + qn if n > 1, and T(n) = p if n = 1, where p and q are constants. The order of this algorithm is
fixed.w: Master theorem: a = 8, b = 2, so n^(log2 8) = n³ dominates qn.

fixed.q: Which of the following algorithms can be used to most efficiently find whether a cycle is present in a given graph?
fixed.w: DFS finds a cycle when it meets a back edge, in O(V + E).

fixed.q: Which of the following algorithms solves the all-pairs shortest path problem?
fixed.w: Floyd-Warshall (Floyd's) finds all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³). Warshall's algorithm computes transitive closure.

fixed.q: The operations of a ______ require that the first element that is inserted is the first one to be removed.
fixed.w: FIFO (first in, first out) is the queue discipline.

fixed.q: Which of the following is true with reference to the Queue data structure in the C programming language? (i) Insertion can take place from the front end. (ii) Deletion can take place from the rear end.
fixed.w: In a queue, insertion is at the rear and deletion at the front. Both statements are reversed, so neither is true.

fixed.q: A stack is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion of elements are done at only one end, known as the top of the stack. The stack holds, from top to bottom: L, M, N, O, P, Q. Which item will be at the top of the stack after removing three items?
fixed.w: Popping L, M and N leaves O on top.

fixed.q: Which data structure is used to indicate that the order of the processing of data must be postponed until other conditions are fulfilled?
fixed.w: A stack postpones processing: items wait (LIFO) until the conditions for processing them are met, as in recursion and backtracking.

fixed.q: What is the polish notation of the given infix expression? (A * B + C)/(E – F * G)
fixed.w: Prefix of (A*B + C) is +*ABC and of (E − F*G) is −E*FG, so the whole expression is /+*ABC−E*FG.

fixed.q: A recursive problem like Tower of Hanoi can be rewritten without recursion using:
fixed.w: Recursion uses the call stack, so an explicit stack can replace it.

fixed.q: Stack data structures are also called ______ list.
fixed.w: A stack is a LIFO (last in, first out) list.

fixed.q: What is the minimum number of stacks of size n required to implement a queue of size n?
fixed.w: A queue can be built from two stacks.

fixed.q: Which of the following can be the valid balance factor of any node in an AVL tree?
fixed.w: In an AVL tree the balance factor must be −1, 0 or +1.

fixed.q: Which statement(s) is/are correct regarding node N deletion in binary search tree? I. If node N has no children then just replace location of N in the parent node by the null pointer. II. If node N has two children, then replace it by preorder successor.
fixed.w: A leaf is simply replaced by NULL, but a node with two children is replaced by its inorder successor, not its preorder successor. So only I.

fixed.q: Which statement is correct regarding binary search tree? I. The value at node N is less than every value in the left subtree of node. II. The value at node N is greater than or equal to every value in the right subtree of N.
fixed.w: In a BST, N is greater than the values in its left subtree and less than or equal to those in its right subtree. Both statements are reversed.

fixed.q: When we perform inorder traversal on a binary tree, we get the ascending-order array. The tree is:
fixed.w: Inorder traversal of a BST gives keys in sorted order.

fixed.q: A binary search tree contains the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. The tree is traversed in preorder and the values are printed out. Which of the following sequences is a valid output?
fixed.w: In D, after root 5 the left subtree 3 1 2 4 is valid, and the right subtree 7 6 8 has 6 left of 7 and 8 right of 7. A puts 6 after 8 in 7's subtree, B contains 9, and C places 1 after 4 in 3's subtree.

fixed.q: What are the data structures categorised as a linear list?
fixed.w: An array (like linked lists, stacks and queues) is a linear list; trees and graphs are non-linear.

fixed.q: What is the total number of elements in a array E[–4 : 1, 6 : 10]?
fixed.w: Rows −4…1 give 6 and columns 6…10 give 5, so 6 × 5 = 30 elements.

fixed.q: Finding the location of the element with a given value is:
fixed.w: Locating an element by value is searching.

fixed.q: A program P reads in 500 integers in the range [0..100] representing the scores of 500 students. It then prints the frequency of each score above 50. What would be the best way for P to store the frequencies?
o: A dynamically allocated array of 550 numbers
fixed.w: Only scores 51-100 (50 values) need counters, so an array of 50 is enough (GATE 2005).

fixed.q: Sparse matrices have
o: Many zero entries than non-zero entries
Many non-zero entries than zero entries
fixed.w: A sparse matrix has many more zero entries than non-zero ones.

fixed.q: Which of the following is not true for tree and graph?
fixed.w: A tree by definition is acyclic, so "tree can have a cycle" is false. Note that B ("a graph is a tree") is also false in general; C is the intended answer.

fixed.q: In an undirected graph, if we add the degrees of all vertices, it is:
o: always n+1, where n is the number of nodes
fixed.w: Handshaking lemma: the sum of degrees = 2 × edges, which is always even.

fixed.q: Which of the following is not used to calculate Hash functions?
fixed.w: Folding, division and mid-square are hash functions; rehashing is a collision-resolution technique.

fixed.q: Inserting a node at the beginning of a singly linked list takes:
fixed.w: Only the head pointer and the new node's next pointer change.

fixed.q: Accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list takes:
o: O(k), i.e. O(n) in the worst case
fixed.w: You must follow the links from the head; there is no random access.

fixed.q: In a circular singly linked list:
o: The last node points back to the first node
The last node points to NULL
fixed.w: This lets you traverse the list repeatedly from any node.

fixed.q: A loop (cycle) in a linked list is typically detected using:
o: Floyd's slow and fast pointer method
fixed.w: If a fast pointer (2 steps) ever meets a slow pointer (1 step), there is a cycle.

fixed.q: Deleting the last node of a singly linked list when only the head pointer is given takes:
fixed.w: You must reach the second-last node to set its next pointer to NULL.

fixed.q: Which data structure is best for implementing a browser's back and forward navigation?
fixed.w: Each page needs links to both its previous and next page.

fixed.q: A collision in hashing occurs when:
o: Two different keys map to the same index
The hash function returns a negative value
fixed.w: Collisions are resolved by chaining or by open addressing.

fixed.q: In separate chaining, each slot of the hash table stores:
o: A linked list of all keys that hash to that slot
A binary search tree of the whole table
A pointer to the next empty slot
fixed.w: Open addressing instead stores keys inside the table itself.

fixed.q: Linear probing mainly suffers from:
fixed.w: Long runs of occupied slots form. Quadratic probing reduces this but has secondary clustering.

fixed.q: With h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing, the keys 12, 22 and 32 are inserted into an empty table. Key 32 goes to index:
fixed.w: 12 goes to 2, 22 collides and goes to 3, 32 collides twice and goes to 4.

fixed.q: The load factor of a hash table with n keys and m slots is:
fixed.w: A higher load factor means more collisions.

fixed.q: The average-case time to search in a well-designed hash table is:
fixed.w: The worst case is O(n) if all keys collide.

fixed.q: Binary search can be applied only to:
o: A linked list in O(log n)
fixed.w: Each step relies on order to discard half the elements.

fixed.q: Linear search on an array of n elements needs, in the worst case:
fixed.w: On average a successful search needs about n / 2 comparisons.

fixed.q: Binary search for 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91] examines how many elements (using mid = (low + high) / 2)?
fixed.w: mid 4 holds 16, go right; mid 7 holds 56, go left; mid 5 holds 23, found.

fixed.q: The maximum number of comparisons binary search needs for 1000 sorted elements is:
Interpolation search on uniformly distributed sorted data has an average time of:
fixed.w: It estimates the position from the key's value instead of always taking the middle.

fixed.q: The three steps of divide and conquer are:
fixed.w: Merge sort: split in half, sort each half, merge.

fixed.q: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n solves to:
fixed.w: This is merge sort's recurrence (Master theorem case 2).

fixed.q: Which of these is NOT a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
fixed.w: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbouring elements; it never splits the problem.

fixed.q: The time complexity of Strassen's matrix multiplication is about:
fixed.w: It uses 7 multiplications instead of 8, so T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2), which is n^(log2 7).

fixed.q: Quick sort's worst case O(n^2) occurs when:
o: The pivot is always the smallest or largest element
The pivot is always the median
The array has all distinct elements
fixed.w: For example, an already sorted array with the first element as the pivot.

fixed.q: The recurrence of binary search is:
fixed.w: One half is discarded at each step, which gives O(log n).

theory.Stack & queue:
• Stack LIFO (recursion, function calls, expression conversion/evaluation, undo, DFS). Queue FIFO (BFS, scheduling).
• Infix → postfix: A + B * C → ABC*+.
• Circular queue full: (rear + 1) % n == front.
• Queue from 2 stacks; stack from 2 queues. Priority queue → heap.
theory.Linked list: • Dynamic size, O(1) insert/delete at a known node, O(n) access. Doubly: prev + next. Circular: last → first.
theory.Arrays:
• Row-major A[i][j] = B + (i·n + j)·w; column-major B + (j·m + i)·w. C uses row-major.
• Sparse matrix: mostly zeros.
theory.Trees:
• Height h: max nodes 2^(h+1) − 1; level l has ≤ 2^l nodes. Leaves n0 = n2 + 1.
• Inorder of BST = sorted. Preorder Root-L-R; inorder L-Root-R; postorder L-R-Root. Preorder + inorder determine the tree.
• BST worst O(n); AVL balance factor −1/0/+1 (LL, RR, LR, RL rotations).
• Heap: complete tree; max-heap parent ≥ children; children of i at 2i+1, 2i+2; build O(n), insert/delete O(log n).
theory.Graphs: • BFS/DFS O(V + E) with lists, O(V²) with a matrix. Topological sort only for DAGs.
theory.Hashing:
• Collisions: chaining; open addressing — linear probing (primary clustering), quadratic (secondary), double hashing.
• h(k) = k mod m; probe next slots on collision.
theory.Complexity:
• Order: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.
• O upper, Ω lower, Θ tight.
• Master theorem examples: 2T(n/2)+n → n log n; T(n/2)+1 → log n; 2T(n/2)+1 → n; T(n−1)+n → n²; 2T(n−1)+1 → 2ⁿ. Hanoi: 2ⁿ − 1 moves.
theory.Sorting:
• Bubble/selection/insertion O(n²) (insertion O(n) best; selection fewest swaps). Merge O(n log n) always, O(n) space, stable. Quick O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst, unstable, in-place. Heap O(n log n), in-place, unstable. Counting/radix linear (non-comparison).
• Comparison sorting lower bound Ω(n log n). Stable: bubble, insertion, merge. Unstable: quick, heap, selection.
theory.Searching: • Binary search: ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons worst case.
theory.Greedy: • Kruskal (cheapest edge, no cycle; union-find), Prim (grow tree), Dijkstra (no negative edges), Huffman, fractional knapsack, activity selection.
theory.Dynamic programming: • Needs overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure. 0/1 knapsack, LCS, matrix chain, Floyd-Warshall O(V³), Bellman-Ford O(VE) (negative edges).
theory.Divide and conquer: • Merge sort, quick sort, binary search, Strassen (independent subproblems).
theory.P vs NP: • P ⊆ NP; P = NP unknown. NP-complete: SAT (Cook), 3-SAT, TSP (decision), vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, 0/1 knapsack (decision).
